item.title: Trump Called for ‘De-Escalation’ in Minneapolis. It Didn’t Last Long.
item.description:
Under fire for the deadly, chaotic federal crackdown in Minneapolis, President Trump this week signaled that he might be open to changing course.

“We’re going to de-escalate a little bit,” Mr. Trump told reporters on Tuesday, trying to calm a mounting crisis after federal agents shot and killed two U.S. citizens in less than a month.

And while Mr. Trump has taken some steps to rein in the tactics of federal agents, he reverted almost immediately to saying he would not pull back the operation, “not at all.” Even amid calls for calming tensions, Mr. Trump issued a social media post at 1:26 a.m. on Friday calling one of the victims, Alex Pretti — a 37-year-old U.S. citizen whom federal agents shot repeatedly — an “agitator and, perhaps, insurrectionist.”

The president’s dueling messages, of de-escalation and doubling down, are part of a pattern during times of political pressure and crisis, when he seems to dial back his impulses temporarily before appearing to decide that he was right all along.

Under pressure from his advisers in the days after a mob attacked the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, Mr. Trump released a video saying he “unequivocally” condemned the “calamity.” He said that those who had taken part “will be brought to justice.” The president now celebrates the Jan. 6 rioters, and one of his first decisions when he took office for a second time was to issue a sweeping grant of clemency to those involved in the assault.

There was a similar back-and-forth after the bloody rallies in Charlottesville, Va., during his first term. Mr. Trump initially was reluctant to condemn white nationalists or neo-Nazi slogans, but ultimately bowed to pressure from his aides and did so. A day later, he reverted to blaming “both sides” for the deadly violence.

The whipsaw approach suggests that for Mr. Trump, crisis communication is dictated by the optics of the moment. Alyssa Farah Griffin, Mr. Trump’s former White House strategic communications director, said that the president was following “the political winds of the right.”

She said Mr. Trump had softened his tone on Minneapolis earlier this week “because the public sentiment even on the right had so clearly shifted.” When the uproar over the shootings was growing — and the federal government’s narrative about Mr. Pretti was beginning to unravel — Mr. Trump tried to distance himself from the statements of his top officials.

But she said she knew “it would only be a matter of time before he’d flip right back to his old rhetoric” after new videos emerged showing Mr. Pretti spitting and cursing at federal agents 11 days before he was shot dead on the street.

In his early morning social media post, Mr. Trump wrote: “Alex Pretti’s stock has gone way down with the just released video of him screaming and spitting in the face of a very calm and under control ICE Officer, and then crazily kicking in a new and very expensive government vehicle, so hard and violent, in fact, that the taillight broke off in pieces.”

It is too early to say whether Mr. Trump’s efforts to reset the situation in Minnesota will result in a significant change on the ground, even as he signals that he is not willing to retreat. When asked on Thursday night if he was pulling back the operation in the state, Mr. Trump said, “No, no. Not at all.”

Still, Mr. Trump pulled out Gregory Bovino, the Border Patrol official who had been the public face of the deportation campaign in Minneapolis and whose aggressive tactics had garnered legal scrutiny.

He sent in his immigration adviser, Tom Homan, who suggested the administration was prepared to soften not only its tone but also its federal deployment.

Local Minnesota officials said on Friday during a news briefing that they were still hearing from constituents, particularly in the Somali community, about federal agents using aggressive tactics.

“I think anyone who’s seen what’s playing out on our streets would say things haven’t” de-escalated, said State Representative Michael Howard, a Democrat. “In a way things have gotten worse and escalated.”

Mr. Homan said he was meeting with state and local officials to discuss a potential agreement related to ICE operations and expanding access to local jails. Such a resolution would allow the administration to “draw down” on the number of federal agents in Minneapolis, Mr. Homan added.

“The hostile rhetoric and dangerous threats and hate must stop,” he said.

Some of Mr. Trump’s hard-right supporters want him to keep fighting.

“There can be no de-escalation at all,” Stephen K. Bannon, who served as the chief White House strategist in Mr. Trump’s first term, said on his podcast, “War Room.”

“You don’t need to bring down the temperature,” Mr. Bannon added. “Raise the temperature.”

Mr. Trump’s conflicting tones come at a sensitive time in Minneapolis and on Capitol Hill. Hours before his post about Mr. Pretti on social media, Senate Democrats reached a deal with Mr. Trump and Republicans to fund most of the government and buy more time to negotiate over Democratic demands to rein in federal immigration agents.

The House must still clear the agreement for Mr. Trump’s signature.

In the hours after Mr. Pretti was pushed to the ground and shot, Mr. Trump joined his top officials in casting blame on the victim. The Department of Homeland Security made the unsubstantiated claim that Mr. Pretti “wanted to do maximum damage and massacre law enforcement.” Mr. Trump took a similar reflexive approach in the hours after a federal agent shot and killed Renee Good, another U.S. citizen, earlier this month.

But after fielding calls from allies over the weekend who warned him that the images of his federal crackdown were only hurting him, Mr. Trump decided to send Mr. Homan to Minneapolis, and the White House tried to distance the president from the rhetoric of Ms. Noem and others.

On Friday, the Justice Department did announce that it would conduct a civil rights investigation into the death of Mr. Pretti, a demand of many critics of the administration calling for more accountability.

At the same time, the Justice Department’s arrest of two journalists — Don Lemon and Georgia Fort — in connection with a disruption at a church that involved an ICE official serving as a pastor, prompted condemnation from Minnesota officials. Rather than respect the traditional independence of the Justice Department, the official White House social media account celebrated the arrest.

“Arresting the storytellers does not change the story,” said Keith Ellison, Minnesota’s Democratic attorney general. “This dangerous, unlawful and unconstitutional surge must end.”

Protesters faced off against federal and local officials outside a federal building in Minneapolis on Friday. The public show of resistance was likely to spread with anti-ICE demonstrations planned across the country this weekend.

“In any moment of crisis when Donald Trump has been tested to meet the moment and bring down the temperature, he has failed every time,” said Sarah Matthews, a deputy White House press secretary in Mr. Trump’s first term who resigned in protest after the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. “He is quite literally incapable of doing that. All he does is add fuel to the fire."

“Trump,” she added, “just can’t help himself.”
